title: The forger's playbook — and its weak points
summary: Four tests every fake must pass, the tricks used to pass each one, and the red flags that recur.

shots.title:
Four tests every
fake must pass.
shots.subtitle: The eye, the lab, the archive, the market.
shots.narration: Think like a forger. To succeed, a fake has to pass four tests: the expert's eye, the laboratory, the archive and the market. Every forger we've met failed at least one.
The eye judges style. The lab tests materials and age. The archive checks the paper trail. And the market decides whether anyone asks hard questions at all.

shots.text: Supply what the experts are **hoping for**.
shots.narration: Beating the eye is easier when you supply what experts hope to find. Beltracchi painted works recorded in old catalogues but long lost, so a 'rediscovery' felt like confirmation.
To beat the lab, forgers reuse old supports. Van Meegeren and de Hory scraped old paintings; Beltracchi bought frames and supports at antique markets. The support then dates correctly.

Ageing is hard to fake: forgery researchers count cracks among the most difficult features to mimic. A 3D study found genuine cracks square in section and as deep as the paint layer; an expert forger's were simpler V-shaped grooves.

shots.text: A good **story** explains away a missing history.
shots.narration: The archive is beaten with stories: a Hungarian aristocrat, a Swiss client who never existed, a famous screenwriter's storage unit. Each explains why a masterpiece has no history.
The market is the forger's ally. When an artist's prices rise or a major study appears, unknown works surface — and buyers who want them to be real stop asking questions.

shots.heading: Red flags that recur
items: An unknown work by an expensive artist
Labels and certificates instead of records
A price — or a profit — too good to be true
shots.narration: From these cases, a checklist of recurring red flags: an unknown work by a pricey artist, an untraceable owner, labels instead of records, an implausible price, and no scientific examination.
Remember the asymmetry. One failed test can expose a fake, but passing one test proves little. Real authentication combines all four.

steps.title: Which test would catch it?
steps.brief: For each weakness, which line of defence is most likely to catch it: the expert's eye, the laboratory, or the archive?

cards.text: A 'Hals' whose brushwork is smooth and timid where the master's is bold.
cards.why: A stylistic mismatch — what connoisseurship is good at.

cards.text: A painting dated 1914 containing a white pigment first made in 1937.
cards.why: The Campendonk case: a material anachronism.

cards.text: A gallery label from a collection that never used labels.
cards.why: Checking the dealer's practice and records exposes it.

cards.text: Records inserted into a museum archive by the seller.
cards.why: Cross-checking other copies and sources reveals the insertion, as in the Drewe case.
Modern instrumental analysis readily identifies Bakelite.

cards.text: A canvas consistent with 1866 but oil that grew in the 1980s.
cards.why: Radiocarbon dating of the binder, as in the Trotter study.

cards.text: A former owner who appears in no inventory or sale catalogue.
cards.why: Provenance is built from inventories, catalogues and other documents.

questions.prompt: Which are classic provenance red flags?
options: An anonymous owner who cannot be traced
A sale-catalogue entry with matching dimensions
A gallery label with no supporting records
questions.explain: Untraceable owners and unsupported labels recur in the Knoedler and Beltracchi cases; matching documents are what you want.

questions.prompt: Why do forgers reuse old canvases and panels?
options: So the support dates correctly and distracts from the new paint
Because old wood holds paint better
questions.explain: It defeats tests that look only at the support — so date the paint too.

questions.prompt: A painting passes one test — say, no anachronistic pigment. On its own, this means…
questions.explain: Consistency with a date is not proof of authorship.

steps.title: Casebook: your red-flag checklist
steps.brief: Start your examiner's casebook with the checklist you will apply for the rest of the course. Be specific: each flag should say what to look for and which test (eye, lab, archive, market) it belongs to.
